body:
Elliot Price: Hey folks — need quick alignment on wording in the hardware tuning profiles docs. The current draft uses “expected behavior” but a couple sections read like guarantees (e.g. “improves p95” / “prevents OOMs”). Want to lock language before we merge PR-903.

Kira Thompson: +1. Runbook side we also want to be super explicit what is a contract/SLA vs what is “observed in our benchmarks”. Otherwise oncall gets paged for “docs said X”.

Marissa Cole: Product POV: we should not imply anything that looks like a promise across all workloads. But we *do* want it to feel actionable, not hand-wavy.

Neha Kapoor: From SRE: please avoid “guarantee”, “ensures”, “prevents”, “will not”. Anything that sounds like “no regressions” will come back during incidents.

Claire Dubois: Agree. Benchmark reports can say “measured” and cite the workload matrix + conditions. Docs can say “expected under workload envelope W”.

Elliot Price: Concrete examples from draft:
1) “H100 balanced profile improves p95 latency by 10–15%”
2) “L40S guardrails prevent OOMs under long context”
3) “B200 profile provides best throughput”

Elliot Price: Proposed rephrase pattern:
- “In Redwood’s workload matrix, we observed …”
- “Expected to … for workloads similar to …”
- “May regress … trade-off …”
- “Not an SLA; for SLA see Dedicated contract / platform SLO page”

Dr. Maya Srinivasan: +1 on tying every claim to a workload envelope. Also call out model interactions (quantization, tool-calling, streaming) because behavior changes.

Noah Patel: We should add a one-paragraph “Scope of claims” section near the top. Something like:
“Profiles are safe-by-default presets. They do not change API semantics. Performance characteristics depend on model family, sequence-length distribution, concurrency, and hardware/driver stack.”

Paula Mendes: Also add explicit rollback guidance language: “If tail latency regresses beyond threshold, disable profile via X”. That helps show it’s operational guidance not a promise.

Kira Thompson: On (2) “prevent OOMs” is a hard no. We can say “reduce OOM risk” and list known failure modes. E.g. memory fragmentation + long context + high concurrency.

Neha Kapoor: Yup. “Guardrails reduce the probability of OOM by enforcing KV-cache budget and queue limits; OOMs are still possible.”

Claire Dubois: For (1) we can say: “Observed p95 improvements of 8–14% across workloads A/B/C; in streaming-heavy workloads we saw neutral to +3% p95 with slightly lower throughput.” More honest.

Marissa Cole: I’d like a consistent template per profile section:
- Intended workload envelope
- What we expect to improve
- Known trade-offs
- How to detect issues
- How to roll back

Elliot Price: That’s great. I can standardize the H100/L40S/B200 reference pages to that structure.

Connor O'Brien: Release train note: wording matters for backports too. If a change is behind a flag, say it. If default changes in runtime-1.x, say “default as of runtime 1.x.y” not “always”.

Noah Patel: For B200 especially: we need “Experimental” stamped everywhere + “subject to change” + explicit stack requirements. Also avoid “best throughput” — say “targeting throughput-first” or “tuned for throughput in initial bring-up”.

Dr. Maya Srinivasan: And please avoid “quality unchanged” unless we’ve actually run evals. We can say “does not intentionally change model outputs; may affect latency/timeouts which can impact application behavior.”

Elliot Price: Good catch. I’ll remove “quality unchanged” line.

Kira Thompson: Can we add a “Not a contractual guarantee” sentence verbatim? Something like:
“Performance numbers are informational only and not a guarantee; Redwood SLAs (if any) are defined in your contract.”

Neha Kapoor: That’s the right direction. Keep it short though — no legal essay in engineering docs.

Claire Dubois: Also suggest we link to the workload matrix doc and define terms:
- p50/p95 measured at gateway vs runtime
- tokens/sec definition (decode only vs total)
- what “streaming stability” means

Marissa Cole: Re: “expected behavior vs guarantees” — I’d keep “Expected behavior” as the header but include a “How to interpret this section” blurb.

Elliot Price: Draft blurb proposal:
“Expected behavior describes what Redwood observed in internal benchmarks and what operators should generally anticipate *within the stated workload envelope*. Real-world results may differ. Use these sections to set rollout guardrails, not to define customer-facing guarantees.”

Paula Mendes: +1. And we should be explicit about “trade-offs”: e.g. throughput-first may worsen tail latency, and fairness knobs can impact streaming.

Noah Patel: One more: avoid “safe” unqualified. Say “safe-by-default for supported configurations” and list what’s “supported” (single node vs multi-GPU, MIG, etc).

Kira Thompson: +1. MIG and multi-GPU are exactly where folks get surprised.

Elliot Price: Action items I’ll take:
- Replace absolute verbs (“prevents/ensures/guarantees”) with observed/expected language
- Add top-level “Scope of claims / not an SLA” note
- Standardize per-profile template + explicit workload envelope
- Add a small glossary for metrics definitions + link to workload matrix
- Mark B200 as Experimental everywhere + remove “best” phrasing

Neha Kapoor: Works. When you update, please @ me for a quick skim before merge.

Dr. Maya Srinivasan: Same, happy to skim for “quality”/evals wording.

Claire Dubois: Ping me too; I’ll make sure the benchmark references are accurate.

Elliot Price: Will do. Updating PR-903 now.

Marissa Cole: :thumbsup: Thanks. This will save us a lot of back-and-forth later.

Connor O'Brien: :thumbsup: also please add the runtime version qualifiers; we’ve been burned by doc drift.

Elliot Price: ack — will anchor claims to “profile pack vX + runtime vY” where possible.
